capex_override.ack_reason: The out-of-band flag is mechanical only: the band is computed against the last FILED capex value under a tag the engine reads, and Snap-on has never filed capex under any such tag (last_filed_value is null), so every value flags out-of-band. This is not an estimate lacking an anchor — it is the exact FY2025 figure from the filer's own 10-K cash-flow statement (see source), corroborated in companyfacts under PaymentsForCapitalImprovements.
capex_override.reason: DATA_GAP:capex — capex missing for FY2023, FY2024, FY2025 (engine labels the Jan-2026 year 2026) in EDGAR companyfacts under every candidate tag the engine reads, because Snap-on reports capex only under PaymentsForCapitalImprovements. The engine applies this single FY2025 filing value to every missing period; against the same statement's true per-year values it understates FY2023 capex by $19.0M (true $95.0M) and FY2024 by $7.5M (true $83.5M), raising those years' OE by ~1.9% / ~0.7% — disclosed, not hidden; the binding base is the TTM base (STALE_FY), where the same value sits only $1.7M below the true filed-leg TTM capex of $77.7M (FY2025 $76.0M − H1 2025 $42.6M + H1 2026 $44.3M, 10-Qs under the same tag), ~0.2% of TTM OE.
capex_override.source: Form 10-K for fiscal year ended January 3, 2026 (filed 2026-02-12, accession 0000091440-26-000045), Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows, investing activities line 'Capital expenditures' tagged us-gaap:PaymentsForCapitalImprovements (a tag the engine does not read): $76.0M for FY2025, with $83.5M for FY2024 and $95.0M for FY2023 in the same statement; corroborated in EDGAR companyfacts under PaymentsForCapitalImprovements with identical values

moat_against: Franchisee dependence — franchisee failure hits sales, collections and finance receivables
Big-ticket tool demand is discretionary and moves with technician confidence and hours
Premium pricing faces lower-cost rivals (Harbor Freight, Milwaukee, Matco/Cornwell)
EV/ADAS shift needs constant diagnostics reinvestment; fewer mechanical repairs per vehicle over time
Captive finance carries credit-cycle risk — loan-loss provisions rise in downturns
Mature end markets — 3-yr revenue CAGR under 2%
moat_for: ~60% share of US mobile tool distribution; franchise van network with sticky weekly in-person sales
Premium brand with proven pricing power — gross margin above 50%
Captive Financial Services flywheel financing franchisees and technicians, locking in the channel
Diagnostics and repair-information systems (software, data, OEM dealership tools) diversify beyond hand tools
Net cash balance sheet; owner's earnings positive 5 of the last 5 fiscal years
moat_justification: Strong moat: dominant (~60%) share of US mobile tool distribution through a franchise van network whose weekly in-person, consultative sales are notoriously sticky; a century-old premium brand with proven pricing power (gross margin above 50%); and a captive Financial Services arm that finances both franchisees and technicians and locks the channel together. Diagnostics/repair-information adds software and data exposure. Erosion forces are real but slow: franchisee dependence, discretionary big-ticket demand tied to technician confidence, lower-cost premium-price competition, the EV/ADAS product shift, finance-receivable credit cycles, and mature end markets growing under 2% on a 3-yr view.
name: Snap-on Inc
one_liner: High-quality premium tool franchise, moat 7/10 — but at $370.65 the weighted IRR is only 8.6% (Tier D, IV@15% $178.36); it clears the 15% hurdle only at roughly half the current price.
